title: Pray and work
hookLine: the Rule of Benedict gives monks set hours for prayer, work and reading (Rule of Benedict 48)
carry: idleness is the enemy of the soul

lines: A DAY IN PIECES, ON PURPOSE.
cards: A bell rings in a monastery. Somewhere a monk sets down a hoe at the edge of a vegetable bed, wipes his hands, and walks to the chapel.

Later another bell, and he walks back to the garden, or to the kitchen, or to a desk with a book open on it. The day isn't one long prayer, and it isn't one long shift. It's divided, on purpose, into pieces.
The plan comes from a book written for monks, the Rule of Saint Benedict. Later readers summed up its way of life in a Latin motto: ora et labora, pray and work.

teach.h: THE MOTTO ISN'T IN THE RULE.
teach.b: First, the motto isn't in the Rule itself.

teach.h: IDLENESS, THE ENEMY OF THE SOUL.
teach.b: The Rule has its own words, and its chapter on daily work opens with a blunt sentence: idleness is the enemy of the soul.

So the brothers should be busy at set times with the work of their hands, and at other set hours with holy reading. The times shift with the seasons, and between them come the hours of prayer the community keeps together.

Second, what the work is for. The Rule says that when monks live by the labor of their hands, as the apostles did, then they are truly monks. Work isn't what they do when prayer is over; it's part of the same life.
If the harvest needs them, they're told not to be upset about going out to gather it. Third, room for the weak. Benedict thinks about the weak brother as well as the strong one.
Those who are sick or delicate, the Rule says, should get work suited to them, so they're neither idle nor crushed by it and driven away.

teach.h: A DAY IN THREE, ON PURPOSE.
teach.b: Fourth, why it reaches past the monastery.
Benedictine monks and nuns still live by this Rule, and some people outside any monastery borrow its shape for their own days.
The insight is simple: when prayer, work and reading each have their own time, none of them swallows the others. The work gets done, the prayer doesn't get skipped, and the mind gets fed.

how: Benedictine monks and nuns live by the Rule of Benedict, keeping set hours of prayer together and set times for work and holy reading; some lay people, called oblates, follow the Rule's shape in ordinary life.

o: the pope who first wrote down the Latin Mass
the saint who founded the first order of friars
the monk whose Rule sets hours for prayer, work, reading

games.q: inside Benedict's Rule — tap the pairs.
p: work suited, not crushed by it
living by the labor of their hands

s: the words ora et labora appear in the Rule of Benedict
they're how later readers summed it up. the Rule puts it in its own words.
the Rule calls idleness the enemy of the soul
it's the opening of the Rule's chapter on daily work.
the Rule expects every monk to do the same heavy work
it says the sick or delicate should get work suited to them, so they aren't crushed and driven away.

games.q: you're a monk, and the harvest is ready but the community is short of hands. the Rule's hours say it's time for reading. what does the Rule say?
o: stay at your reading, the hours are fixed.
go out and gather the harvest, without being upset about it.
pay workers so the monks can keep praying.
games.why: the Rule says if need requires them to gather the harvest themselves, they shouldn't be distressed: living by their own labor is part of being truly monks.

practice: Walk through the rest of your day in your mind and find three small places in it: one for work, one for prayer or stillness, even five minutes, and one for a page of something that feeds you.
Give each a rough time, then let the plan go and just sit, the way a monk might between bells. If you pray, these two minutes can be the first of the three.

wordCard.voice: Saint Benedict. Whose Rule gives monks set hours for prayer, work and reading, so that none of them swallows the others. Today's word.

orig.note: Latin, from the Christian monastic tradition: pray and work, a later motto for the Rule of Benedict.

carryVoice: Your line: idleness is the enemy of the soul. A day in three, kept on purpose. That's day eight hundred ninety.
